The Mphanda Nkuwa hydroelectric project has used the Mozambique–European Union Business Forum 2026 to set out how its generation and transmission plans, paired with a community-development drive, could anchor the country’s renewable ambitions. The project’s implementation office, GMNK, joined the forum alongside the 5th Renewables Business Conference in Mozambique. Represented by its director general, Carlos Yum, the office took part in panels on strategic investment in the energy sector and on the role of large hydropower schemes in the national grid. The sessions weighed Mozambique’s room to expand renewable generation, reinforce network infrastructure and widen access to electricity. Against that backdrop, Yum set out where the Mphanda Nkuwa project now stands, walking delegates through the structuring of its generation and transmission infrastructure. Building the social case alongside the dam Crucially, the office framed Mphanda Nkuwa as more than a generation asset. Yum pointed to the Social Development Plan, a voluntary programme designed to turn the project’s footprint into lasting socio-economic gains. The plan aims to create jobs, strengthen communities and broaden access to power, health, education and agriculture across the families within the project’s reach. The early results are already on the ground. So far, 4,600 people have received basic health care through mobile brigades, 100 women have been trained in nutrition, and three ambulances have been readied for the three host districts of Marara, Chiuta and Cahora Bassa. The programme has also delivered 2,070 complete farming kits, donated sporting equipment, and trained 26 young people from local communities in electrical work. More is planned. The office expects to hand over 500 solar kits, one per household, across the three districts, together with a 27-kilometre medium-voltage line that will carry power deeper into the area. Studies before steel In parallel, the project is running a rigorous review and update of its pre-feasibility studies, including the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment of the generation and transmission works. The exercise is meant to protect the downstream environmental balance, safeguard the needs of communities in the project’s zone of influence, and secure sound land-use planning and public safety. That review is being carried out in line with national legislation and international best practice. title: Zimbabwe Introduces First Crypto Licensing Framework
summary:
Zimbabwe crypto regulation arrives as the FIU begins licensing virtual asset firms. What it means for fintech and capital flows.

full_text: Zimbabwe Introduces First Crypto Licensing Framework Zimbabwe crypto regulation arrives as the FIU begins licensing virtual asset firms. What it means for fintech and capital flows. The post Zimbabwe Introduces First Crypto Licensing Framework appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Zimbabwe crypto regulation has arrived, pulling digital asset activity into the formal economy under direct anti-money laundering oversight for the first time.   Zimbabwe has moved to codify its fast-growing crypto market. Its first specific rules require virtual asset businesses to register with the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) and pay an annual US$500 licensing fee. From informal boom to supervised market Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube issued regulations that oblige any firm buying, selling, transferring, exchanging or safeguarding virtual assets to register every year with the FIU. The FIU sits inside the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe. Registration costs US$500 per annum. Operating without it is now an offence that exposes firms to penalties. The move ends years of legal ambiguity. Authorities barred banks and other financial institutions from dealing in cryptocurrencies in 2018. That pushed activity onto peer-to-peer networks and informal online platforms. Trading volumes grew as Zimbabweans sidestepped the formal system. Many used WhatsApp groups and small brokers rather than licensed intermediaries. Crypto’s rise in Zimbabwe is closely tied to macro conditions. Years of high inflation, repeated currency changes and low confidence in formal banking pushed households and small businesses towards dollar-linked or crypto-linked instruments. Bitcoin and other digital assets gained traction as alternative stores of value. They also offered a way to keep savings outside the domestic monetary system. Remittances have been another driver. Zimbabwe’s large diaspora has looked for cheaper, faster channels than traditional money transfer operators. Crypto rails, combined with local peer-to-peer cash-out networks, offered lower fees and better FX rates in many cases. As a result, digital assets are now embedded in how part of the economy manages both savings and cross-border transfers. Regulation changes the risk calculus for that ecosystem. Licensing creates a defined perimeter for supervision. It gives the state better visibility over flows that were previously opaque. It also signals to international partners that Zimbabwe is aligning more closely with global anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist-financing standards. Reading the signal for fintech and capital flows Zimbabwe now joins a growing group of African markets that have moved from blanket banking bans or informal toleration to explicit crypto rules. South Africa treats most crypto assets as financial products under its Financial Sector Conduct Authority regime. Nigeria has shifted from restrictive guidance to a more structured licensing push. Kenya and Mauritius are both advancing supervisory frameworks for virtual asset service providers. Chainalysis estimates that Sub-Saharan Africa recorded more than US$205 billion in crypto transaction value between July 2024 and June 2025. That marks a 52% year-on-year increase. This growth, alongside persistent inflation and exchange-rate pressures in several economies, suggests that digital assets will remain part of the region’s financial architecture rather than a short-lived arbitrage. Industry reaction inside Zimbabwe has been cautiously positive. Harare-based trader Jeffrey Mutambiranwa said the framework helps traders operate openly rather than “underground”. He welcomed the chance to work within a clear rulebook. For local platforms, a modest US$500 fee is unlikely to be prohibitive. It instead acts as a basic filter for serious operators. It also opens a gateway to formal engagement with banks, payment providers and potential institutional partners. For investors, the new rules send a useful signal. Zimbabwe is not opening the floodgates to unrestricted capital flows. However, it is normalising a parallel market that citizens already use as a hedge and a remittance rail. That balance between capital control, consumer demand and compliance oversight will shape how far regulated exchanges, wallet providers and cross-border payments firms can scale. The next phase will be crucial. Investors should watch how the FIU interprets its mandate in practice, whether secondary rules follow on custody, stablecoins and token listings, and how banks respond to licensed crypto businesses that now sit inside the formal regulatory perimeter. In a high-inflation market where digital assets already act as a de facto store of value, this Zimbabwe crypto regulation could be an early marker of broader financial normalisation and a test case for fintech models across the region. Biya’s extended rule has also drawn renewed scrutiny, as explored in Africa Briefing’s report on how Biya’s eighth term sparked Cameroon tension. Government authorities have previously defended their actions as necessary to maintain public order and national security. French authorities will first determine whether the complaint satisfies the legal requirements for further action. Even if accepted for review, there is no guarantee that a formal investigation or prosecution will follow. For now, the principal development is procedural: French judicial authorities have received a complaint from a Cameroonian opposition figure. According to officials, the measures target individuals found to be in the country without the required legal documentation, while legal experts and rights advocates continue to stress the importance of due process and compliance with constitutional and international obligations. Migration remains politically sensitive Immigration has become a contentious issue in South Africa, with concerns over unemployment, service delivery and border management fuelling calls for stricter enforcement. The issue has gained further prominence alongside a growing anti-migrant movement ahead of local elections, adding political pressure to government efforts. At the same time, civil society organisations have urged authorities to ensure that enforcement actions are carried out lawfully and without undermining the rights of refugees, asylum seekers or other people entitled to protection under South African or international law. The debate has also highlighted the need to distinguish clearly between undocumented migrants and foreign nationals who are legally residing, working or studying in the country. Figures relate to undocumented migrants The government’s reported total applies to people whom authorities identified as lacking legal permission to remain in South Africa. Officials have not indicated that the operation targets documented migrants or individuals with lawful immigration status. South Africa has historically attracted migrants from neighbouring countries and elsewhere on the continent because it has offered relatively greater economic opportunities than many states in the region. At the same time, economic pressures and political tensions have placed migration policy under increasing public scrutiny. Wider regional significance The latest figures reflect broader challenges facing governments across southern Africa as they seek to balance border management, labour mobility and regional integration commitments. The regional dimension has previously been underscored by events such as Ghana’s evacuation of citizens following attacks in South Africa, highlighting how migration-related tensions can affect neighbouring countries. Keypoints: Ghana’s economy expanded 6.4 percent in the first quarter of 2026, extending its post-crisis recovery Inflation has fallen from more than 22 percent in January 2025 to 3.4 percent, while the Tema Oil Refinery has resumed refining Jubilee crude Sustaining the recovery will depend on creating jobs, boosting incomes and reducing reliance on commodity-driven growth GHANA’S economy has undergone a dramatic transformation since emerging from the severe fiscal and currency crisis that forced it to seek IMF support and restructure its debt. The latest figures from the Ghana Statistical Service show GDP expanded by 6.4 percent in the first quarter of 2026, reinforcing the country’s position as one of Africa’s strongest post-crisis performers. The headline numbers are encouraging, but they tell only part of the story. The real measure of success will be whether macroeconomic gains improve the lives of ordinary Ghanaians through better jobs, higher incomes and stronger purchasing power. Stability has returned to the economy The scale of Ghana’s recovery is striking. Inflation, which stood above 22 percent when President John Mahama returned to office in January 2025, has fallen sharply to 3.4 percent. Foreign exchange reserves have strengthened, the cedi has stabilised and investor confidence has improved significantly. These achievements reflect both prudent macroeconomic management and the continuation of reforms supported by the IMF. They also provide a more predictable environment for businesses planning long-term investment. Gold is powering the rebound One of the administration’s defining economic strategies has been leveraging Ghana’s position as Africa’s leading gold producer. Elevated international prices have boosted export earnings and strengthened external balances, with Ghana’s surge in gold export earnings providing valuable support for the wider recovery. At the centre of this strategy is GoldBod, established to formalise artisanal gold trading and increase domestic value capture. As Africa Briefing has previously reported in its analysis of GoldBod’s landmark refining agreement, the initiative aims to strengthen oversight while maximising returns from Ghana’s mineral wealth. The longer-term ambition extends beyond exports. Research on GoldBod’s potential to reshape Ghana’s economy suggests the institution could become a key pillar of fiscal resilience if successfully implemented. Energy revival strengthens confidence The government has also sought to revitalise the petroleum sector by improving relations with investors and supporting new production. A major milestone has been the revival of the Tema Oil Refinery, which has resumed refining crude sourced from the Jubilee Field after years of limited operations. The restart marks a significant step towards increasing domestic value addition and reducing dependence on imported refined products. The broader objective is to ensure Ghana extracts greater economic value from its natural resources while strengthening industrial capacity. Private investment signals renewed optimism Economic recovery is also becoming visible beyond government statistics. Corporate activity and investor sentiment have improved as confidence returns to the market. The successful public offering by Kasapreko offered a notable example. As highlighted in Africa Briefing’s analysis of Kasapreko’s IPO and renewed investor confidence, strong demand reflected growing optimism about Ghana’s economic outlook and the country’s improving business environment. Meanwhile, Mahama’s broader industrial ambitions, including the government’s 24-hour economy strategy, are intended to convert macroeconomic stability into manufacturing growth, export expansion and job creation. Challenges remain despite the progress Despite impressive gains, Ghana’s recovery is not guaranteed. The economy remains exposed to fluctuations in global commodity prices, particularly gold, while the energy sector continues to pose fiscal risks through accumulated liabilities. Infrastructure investment, healthcare spending and education funding will also require disciplined fiscal management if public finances are to remain sustainable. Most importantly, many households have yet to experience the benefits reflected in national statistics. Years of elevated inflation eroded purchasing power, and rebuilding living standards will take time even as price growth moderates. The next phase is about prosperity Ghana has largely succeeded in restoring macroeconomic stability after a period of exceptional turmoil. Growth is accelerating, inflation has fallen dramatically and confidence among investors is returning. The challenge now is ensuring those gains reach citizens across the country. If the government can convert stronger economic fundamentals into sustained employment, rising incomes and inclusive development, Ghana could become a leading example of successful post-crisis reform in Africa. If it cannot, impressive GDP figures alone may prove insufficient to convince the public that the recovery is complete.The post Ghana’s recovery enters its defining moment first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Governments are expanding private participation in electricity infrastructure Open-access reforms aim to improve grid efficiency and attract investment Strong regulation remains essential to deliver reliable and affordable power AFRICAN governments are increasingly turning to private investment and regulatory reform to modernise electricity systems as rising demand and fiscal constraints challenge traditional state-led models. The trend reflects a broader shift in thinking about how power markets should operate across the continent. Rather than relying solely on publicly funded utilities to generate, transmit and distribute electricity, policymakers are exploring frameworks that encourage competition, independent investment and regional cooperation. In an opinion article, Shirley Webber and Nikhil Kasiram of Absa Corporate and Investment Banking argue that these developments are creating new opportunities for infrastructure finance and long-term economic growth. Their analysis, published by Engineering News, suggests that regulatory reform and greater private-sector participation are reshaping Africa’s electricity landscape. This Africa Briefing article expands on those arguments with additional policy context and independent analysis. Why the reforms matter The debate over Africa’s electricity future is no longer confined to building new power plants. Increasing attention is being paid to how electricity moves across transmission networks, how independent producers connect to national grids and how regulators can create markets that encourage investment while protecting consumers. Many countries continue to face electricity shortages, ageing infrastructure and constrained public finances. Opening parts of the sector to private participation could help mobilise capital that governments alone may struggle to provide, particularly for large-scale transmission projects and renewable energy integration. Institutions such as the International Energy Agency and the African Development Bank have repeatedly highlighted the scale of investment needed to expand reliable electricity access and support economic development across Africa. The push for new financing models also complements initiatives such as the World Bank-backed $50bn Africa electrification plan, which aims to accelerate access to electricity through coordinated public and private investment. Grid modernisation moves up the agenda Webber and Kasiram argue that Uganda’s Amari Project illustrates growing interest in involving private investors in transmission infrastructure alongside electricity generation. In their view, such initiatives demonstrate that governments are becoming more receptive to diversified financing models for critical energy assets. The authors also highlight reforms in countries including South Africa and Zambia, where policymakers have sought to create frameworks that allow broader participation in electricity markets through transmission upgrades and open-access arrangements. For South Africa, strengthening transmission capacity has become increasingly important as renewable energy projects require new grid connections. Expanding that infrastructure is expected to demand significant investment beyond public resources alone, reflecting trends seen in Kenya’s $311m power transmission partnership and Britain-backed transmission projects in Ethiopia, both of which seek to unlock additional generation through stronger grid networks. Opportunities beyond power generation Webber and Kasiram argue that Africa’s evolving electricity sector presents opportunities extending beyond wind and solar generation to include transmission networks, battery storage, mini-grids and digital technologies that improve system efficiency. These investments could prove especially valuable in underserved regions where extending conventional grid infrastructure is difficult or uneconomical. Decentralised energy solutions may help improve electricity access while supporting local businesses and essential public services. The broader strategy aligns with arguments advanced in ‘Africa must drive its own energy shift’, which emphasises the importance of African-led financing and policy solutions to meet the continent’s long-term energy needs. The development of stronger regional interconnections could also facilitate greater cross-border electricity trade, enabling countries with surplus generation to export power to neighbouring markets facing supply constraints. Challenges remain Despite growing momentum, significant barriers continue to affect the pace of reform. Regulatory uncertainty, financially stressed utilities and inconsistent policy implementation can reduce investor confidence and delay project delivery. Some analysts caution that greater private participation must be accompanied by strong regulation to prevent market concentration, protect consumers and ensure electricity remains affordable while maintaining reliable service. Maintaining affordability while encouraging private investment will require transparent governance, predictable regulation and effective coordination between governments, utilities and commercial developers. Policymakers must also ensure that reforms contribute to broader development goals by improving reliability and expanding access for households and businesses that remain underserved. Outlook Many African electricity markets appear to be entering a period of structural transformation in which governments increasingly act as market enablers rather than sole providers of infrastructure and services. Whether these reforms deliver lasting benefits will depend on the quality of regulation, the expansion of transmission networks and the ability of countries to balance commercial incentives with public policy objectives. If implemented effectively, more open and interconnected electricity markets could strengthen energy security, support industrial growth and accelerate electrification across the continent.The post Africa opens power grids to private investment first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Hartree Metals will provide a $7m financing facility for Hope & Gorob The trader has agreed to purchase 100 percent of the mine’s future copper concentrate The agreement reflects growing confidence in Namibia’s emerging copper industry NAMIBIA’S emerging copper industry has received a major boost after Hartree Metals, a metals trading and financing company and subsidiary of Hartree Partners LP, agreed to provide a $7m financing facility and purchase the entire future copper concentrate output from Bezant Resources’ Hope & Gorob project. The agreement, announced by London AIM-listed mining developer Bezant Resources on June 11, combines development funding with a life-of-mine offtake arrangement covering 100 percent of production from the planned operation. According to the company, first copper concentrate production remains targeted for the third quarter of 2026. Strategic partnership to advance production Bezant Resources, which focuses on developing copper and gold assets across Africa, said the funding will support construction of the Hope & Gorob mine and commissioning of the associated NLZM processing plant. The $7m financing facility will be made available in five tranches and includes an option allowing Hartree Metals to convert part or all of the debt into equity under agreed terms. In exchange, Hartree will purchase all copper concentrate produced over the life of the mine under market-based commercial conditions. Executive chairman Colin Bird said the project remains on schedule and within budget for first production in the third quarter of 2026, describing the agreement as the foundation for what could become a broader long-term partnership in Namibia. Who are Hartree Metals and Bezant Resources? Hartree Metals is part of Hartree Partners LP, a global commodities trading and asset management group headquartered in New York. The company specialises in sourcing, financing, trading and marketing base and precious metals while providing logistics and risk management services to mining operations worldwide. Bezant Resources is an AIM-listed mining company focused on developing copper and gold projects in Africa. Its flagship Hope & Gorob asset is located within Namibia’s Matchless Copper Belt and is expected to become the company’s first producing mine as it transitions from exploration into commercial operations. Namibia’s copper sector gathers momentum The transaction reflects growing confidence in Namibia’s copper potential after years in which the country’s mining industry was dominated by uranium, diamonds and gold. Recent developments build on Namibia’s broader surge in mining exploration activity, which has attracted renewed investor interest amid rising demand for critical minerals. Several projects are progressing alongside Hope & Gorob. Appian Capital Advisory’s planned investment in the Omitiomire copper project is expected to strengthen the country’s ambitions to revive large-scale copper production and expand exports. The large Haib project is also advancing through development studies. At the same time, rising demand linked to electrification, renewable energy infrastructure and electric vehicle manufacturing is encouraging traders and investors to secure copper supply from new mining jurisdictions, reinforcing Africa’s growing strategic importance in global critical minerals supply chains. Opportunity to diversify mining exports If Hope & Gorob and other planned projects move into production as anticipated, Namibia could broaden its mining export base and generate additional tax revenues, foreign exchange earnings and employment opportunities. For Hartree Metals, the agreement secures future concentrate supply from an emerging producer. For Bezant Resources, it provides development capital and a guaranteed customer, reducing commercial risk as the company advances towards first production. The agreement adds momentum to Namibia’s efforts to rebuild its copper industry at a time when global demand for the metal is expected to rise. If projects such as Hope & Gorob reach commercial production, the country could strengthen its position in global critical minerals supply chains while diversifying a mining sector that has long been anchored by uranium, diamonds and gold, further cementing its place among Africa’s emerging critical minerals hotspots.The post Hartree funds Namibia copper project first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: SigraFi will provide structured finance through a revolving working capital facility Partnership aims to formalise artisanal mining and expand traceable exports Around 25,000 miners could benefit from improved access to legal export markets UK-HEADQUARTERED responsible gold sourcing company SigraFi has entered a long-term partnership with PeaceGold Trading Company to expand the supply of traceable artisanal gold from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, introducing structured financing and accredited refining access for cooperative-based producers. The agreement is significant because much of the country’s artisanal gold sector remains outside formal international markets. By combining growth capital with compliant export pathways, the partners aim to improve livelihoods, strengthen supply-chain transparency and reduce illicit trade at a time when gold smuggling in the Democratic Republic of Congo has remained a persistent challenge. Structured finance tied to future deliveries Under the commercial framework, SigraFi will provide structured working capital through a revolving working capital facility linked to future contracted gold deliveries, alongside refinery-delivery support and logistics coordination. In return, participating cooperatives will supply fully traceable gold doré for delivery into accredited international refining channels. The companies said the model combines SigraFi’s compliant sourcing, capital structuring, logistics expertise and refinery relationships with PeaceGold’s work to formalise artisanal mining in eastern DRC. The financing mechanism is designed to offer producers more reliable routes to market, greater pricing transparency and improved access to international refining infrastructure. The partnership also complements broader efforts to modernise the country’s mineral exports, including recent DRC copper shipments through the Lobito Corridor, underscoring increasing investment in secure and transparent export corridors. Supporting responsible mining communities Founded in 2013 by Greg Valerio, PeaceGold works alongside local organisations to legalise artisanal mining operations, reduce mercury use and establish compliant export pathways while supporting peace-building and community development. The initiative currently collaborates with around 11 artisanal mining cooperatives in Ituri Province, representing approximately 25,000 miners and support workers. By linking finance directly to future gold deliveries, the partners hope to reduce reliance on informal traders and help miners retain more value from their production. SigraFi executives have argued that responsible producers frequently struggle to access compliant export channels, refinery relationships and appropriately structured finance despite growing international demand for traceable minerals. Formalising a major informal sector Artisanal and small-scale mining contributes an estimated one-fifth of global gold production and supports millions of livelihoods worldwide. Yet many producers remain excluded from recognised international markets because of financing, compliance and infrastructure barriers. The SigraFi–PeaceGold partnership seeks to address those obstacles by creating a commercially sustainable model that links responsible production with verified supply chains and accredited refiners. Analysts say the agreement reflects a wider trend as Africa assumes a larger role in global mineral supply chains, increasing demand for ethically sourced commodities and transparent procurement practices. A potential blueprint for the continent If successful, the initiative could provide a model for responsible sourcing partnerships elsewhere in Africa and Latin America, where artisanal mining remains a vital source of employment but often lacks access to formal finance and international markets. Comparable reforms are already under way in other jurisdictions, with Burkina Faso tightening oversight of its gold sector through mining code reforms aimed at capturing greater value from domestic mineral production.The post DRC signs UK-backed artisanal gold supply deal first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Marriott has expanded its Caribbean portfolio with a new Barbados resort Tourism contributes about 31.5 percent of Barbados’ GDP and supports around 36,000 jobs African destinations could draw lessons from Barbados’ blend of global branding and local identity MARRIOTT International’s opening of the Turtle Beach Barbados, A Tribute Portfolio All-Inclusive Resort, is highlighting how strategic investment in globally recognised hospitality brands can strengthen tourism-driven economies, offering potential lessons for African countries seeking to attract more visitors and private capital. The launch comes as governments across Africa look to tourism as a catalyst for economic diversification, job creation and foreign exchange earnings. Barbados’ experience suggests that pairing international hospitality expertise with authentic local culture can help destinations compete more effectively in the global travel market. Marriott expands its Caribbean footprint According to Marriott International, the beachfront Turtle Beach property on Barbados’ South Coast has joined the company’s all-inclusive portfolio, adding another internationally recognised brand to one of the Caribbean’s most established holiday destinations. The investment comes as tourism continues to underpin Barbados’ economy. Industry estimates indicate that travel and tourism generate about 31.5 percent of the country’s GDP and support approximately 36,000 jobs, accounting for around 26 percent of total employment on the island. As tourism contributes more than 30 percent of Barbados’ economy, new hospitality investments are closely watched for their wider economic impact. The resort offers suite-style accommodation, multiple restaurants and bars, family-oriented amenities and activities designed to blend the convenience of an all-inclusive stay with experiences rooted in Barbadian culture. The opening also builds on Barbados’ strong tourism rebound as international travel demand continues to recover. Global brands can elevate destination appeal The Barbados project demonstrates how partnerships with established hotel operators can enhance a destination’s visibility among international travellers. Global hospitality companies typically bring extensive marketing networks, reservation systems and loyalty programmes that can attract repeat visitors while introducing new audiences to emerging destinations. For African tourism authorities, such collaborations may provide opportunities to accelerate investment and improve service standards, provided they complement rather than overshadow local businesses and communities. Local identity remains a competitive edge Marriott says the resort incorporates Barbadian influences into its guest experience, illustrating how international investment can coexist with cultural authenticity. That principle is equally relevant in Africa, where countries such as Ghana, Kenya, Morocco, Rwanda and Tanzania continue investing in tourism products centred on heritage, wildlife, gastronomy and community experiences. Marriott’s ambitions also extend across Africa, including a luxury safari debut in Tanzania’s Serengeti and new luxury safari camps in Kenya, underscoring the company’s confidence in experience-led travel markets. Building inclusive tourism economies Tourism specialists often argue that the greatest economic gains come when hotels source goods and services locally, creating opportunities for farmers, artisans, transport providers and tour operators alongside accommodation businesses. Rather than focusing solely on increasing room capacity, governments can strengthen tourism ecosystems that distribute benefits across local communities and encourage sustainable long-term growth. The Barbados example highlights how destination branding, infrastructure investment and community participation can reinforce one another. A blueprint worth adapting The opening of Turtle Beach Barbados represents more than the addition of another luxury resort. It reflects a broader strategy of combining global hospitality expertise with local character to create a compelling tourism product that supports national development. For African countries seeking to expand their visitor economies, the lesson is not to replicate the Caribbean model exactly but to adapt its underlying principles: attract credible investment, showcase authentic culture and ensure local communities share in the rewards of tourism growth.The post Barbados’ new resort offers lessons for African tourism first appeared on Africa Briefing.

A separate person with knowledge of the arrangement told the Associated Press that he remains entitled to payment despite his absence from the six-week tournament. The arrangement would ensure Artan is not financially disadvantaged despite being unable to officiate after being denied entry into the United States. Referee remains positive Following his return to Mogadishu, Artan adopted a measured tone when reflecting on the episode. ‘What happened has happened and it was fate. I am grateful for the support FIFA gave me,’ he told Reuters. He also encouraged young Somalis to remain optimistic, saying: ‘Somalia is ours, whether things are good or bad. Keypoints: FONAREV and CIA-VAR have launched an international petition seeking recognition of decades of atrocities in the DRC The campaign has attracted more than 5,000 verified signatures and aims to advance justice and reparations for victims Organisers say international acknowledgement is essential to accountability and lasting peace TWO Democratic Republic of Congo institutions have launched an international petition calling for formal recognition of decades of atrocities committed in the country, with the campaign already attracting more than 5,000 verified signatures on Change.org. The initiative is being led by the National Fund for Victim Reparations (FONAREV) and the Interministerial Commission for Victim Assistance and Reform Support (CIA-VAR), which argue that international acknowledgement of the violence is a crucial step towards justice, reparations and sustainable peace. Paris launch draws international audience The petition was officially unveiled during La Traversée – The Forgotten Genocide of the DRC, an event held at the end of May at the Pavillon Vendôme in Paris. Several hundred attendees, including political representatives, diplomats, academics, cultural figures, civil society organisations and members of the Congolese diaspora, participated in the launch. According to sources familiar with the initiative, officials from FONAREV and CIA-VAR later travelled to Brussels, where they held discussions with Members of the European Parliament and advisers linked to the European People’s Party, European Conservatives and Reformists, and Patriots for Europe political groups. Campaign centred on ‘Genocost’ The petition urges national governments, regional bodies, international institutions, African organisations and the wider international community to formally acknowledge what its organisers describe as three decades of mass atrocities in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Central to the campaign is the concept of ‘Genocost’, a term incorporated into Congolese law in December 2022. According to FONAREV and CIA-VAR, the concept reflects their view that violence in the country has been driven in part by the illegal exploitation of natural resources for economic gain. The two institutions contend that broader international recognition would strengthen efforts to hold perpetrators accountable while improving access to reparations and support for victims. Humanitarian evidence cited by organisers The organisations point to a range of international reports and studies in support of their campaign. The International Rescue Committee has previously published estimates suggesting that conflict and its indirect consequences in the DRC have contributed to millions of deaths, including an estimated 5.4 million between 1998 and 2003, although methodologies and overall casualty estimates have been the subject of discussion among researchers. Meanwhile, the UN Mapping Report published in 2010 documented hundreds of alleged serious violations committed between 1993 and 2003. The report stated that some incidents, if established before a competent court, could potentially be characterised as acts of genocide under international law, while stressing that judicial proceedings would be required to determine legal responsibility. The humanitarian toll remains severe. Millions of people are internally displaced, while mass graves have been documented in several parts of the country, including Kisangani, Kivu and Ituri. FONAREV says it has registered more than 250,000 victims in the eastern provinces for compensation initiatives and legal support programmes. Supporters call for greater awareness The petition has attracted messages of support from signatories who say the international community should pay greater attention to the suffering endured by Congolese communities. Loic, from Montmorency in France, who attended the Paris launch, wrote: ‘Attending the Genocost event this evening has made me fully aware of the gravity of what has been happening in Congo for more than 30 years. My full support to the victims and all those affected by this tragedy.’ Another supporter, identified as Dedieu, commented: ‘To remain silent is to be complicit in what is happening in Congo.’ Lilas, who said family members live in conflict-affected areas including Goma, called for increased international attention to communities that have endured years of insecurity and violence. Christian, another signatory, argued that crimes committed in the DRC deserve greater international recognition and remembrance. Organisers seek wider international backing A spokesperson for FONAREV described the petition as an effort to mobilise international support for victims and increase awareness of the scale of the humanitarian crisis. ‘We want to raise awareness and engage as many actors in the international community as possible to take a stand and support the vital work being carried out by FONAREV and CIA-VAR in the DRC,’ the spokesperson said. ‘To misname things is to add to the world’s misfortunes. To not name them at all is to deny our humanity, and that is why we created La Traversée.’ The petition remains open on Change.org as campaigners seek broader international support for recognition, justice and remembrance for victims of violence in the Democratic Republic of Congo.  The post DRC petition seeks global recognition of decades of atrocities first appeared on Africa Briefing.
